claims.subject: Neighborhood Sampling Strategy
claims.evidence_quote: We view the problem of sampling neighborhoods of a source node as a form of local search.

claims.subject: Breadth-first Sampling
claims.evidence_quote: The neighborhoodNS is restricted to nodes which are immediate neighbors of the source.

claims.subject: Depth-first Sampling
claims.evidence_quote: The neighborhood consists of nodes sequentially sampled at increasing distances from the source node.

claims.subject: Breadth-first Sampling
claims.evidence_quote: The breadth-first and depth-first sampling represent extreme scenarios in terms of the search space they explore leading to interesting implications on the learned representations.

claims.subject: Depth-first Sampling
claims.evidence_quote: The breadth-first and depth-first sampling represent extreme scenarios in terms of the search space they explore leading to interesting implications on the learned representations.

claims.subject: Homophily
claims.evidence_quote: Under the homophily hypothesis [7, 36] nodes that are highly interconnected and belong to similar network clusters or communities should be embedded closely together ( e.g., nodes s1 and u in Figure 1 belong to the same network community).

claims.subject: Structural Equivalence
claims.evidence_quote: In contrast, under the structural equivalence hypothesis [10] nodes that have similar structural roles in networks should be embedded closely together ( e.g., nodes u and s6 in Figure 1 act as hubs of their corresponding communities).

claims.subject: Structural Equivalence
claims.evidence_quote: Importantly, unlike homophily, structural equivalence does not emphasize connectivity; nodes could be far apart in the network and still have the same structural role.
